subject: Yamamura et al. (1973)
object: Yamamura et al. (1973) described paralysis agitans (parkinsonism) with early onset and marked diurnal fluctuation of symptoms.

subject: Mitsui et al. (1994)
object: Mitsui et al. (1994) reported 2 sibs with hereditary parkinsonism accompanied by pyramidal signs and cerebellar ataxia. Anticholinergic drugs had a dramatic beneficial effect in both sibs, but levodopa did not. The authors proposed this as a new hereditary variant of early-onset Parkinson disease, distinct from the levodopa-sensitive forms of juvenile Parkinson disease.

subject: Mitsui et al. (1994)
object: Mitsui et al. (1994) noted that the response to anticholinergics in their sibs resembled the response reported in patients with Joseph disease. They suggested that it pointed to dysfunction of an 'indirect pathway' involving the globus pallidus and the subthalamic nucleus, in addition to dysfunction of the nigrostriatal system.

subject: Bonifati et al. (1994)
object: Bonifati et al. (1994) reported anticipation of onset age in familial Parkinson disease.

subject: Takahashi et al. (1994)
object: Takahashi et al. (1994) described a family in which 4 of 5 sibs developed parkinsonism with similar onset at an early age. The parkinsonism improved following sleep. The parents were first cousins.

subject: Takahashi et al. (1994)
object: Takahashi et al. (1994) reported affected sibs born to first-cousin parents in a family with juvenile parkinsonism.

subject: Takahashi et al. (1994)
object: Takahashi et al. (1994) reported the autopsy of one affected sib, a 67-year-old woman. Pathologic changes were confined to the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNPC) and the locus ceruleus. The medial and ventrolateral SNPC showed obvious neuronal loss and gliosis. Elsewhere in the SNPC and in the locus ceruleus, neurons were fewer and most had low melanin content, with no detectable gliosis or extraneuronal free melanin. There were no Lewy bodies, and the authors concluded that the overall pathology differed from that of Lewy body Parkinson disease.

subject: Ishikawa and Miyatake (1995)
object: Ishikawa and Miyatake (1995) reported a family with hereditary juvenile dystonia-parkinsonism in which 8 members in 3 generations were affected, consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. The authors considered the patients to have a specific form of hereditary dystonia-parkinsonism.

subject: Ishikawa and Miyatake (1995)
object: Ishikawa and Miyatake (1995) described 8 affected members of 1 family with juvenile dystonia-parkinsonism. They had parkinsonism, sleep benefit, a marked response to levodopa, wearing-off phenomenon and levodopa-induced choreic dyskinesia. The patients also had neck dystonia (torticollis and retrocollis), foot dystonia and other dystonic movements, such as frequently lifting the thigh. In 1 patient the main feature was dystonic movement, which worsened after levodopa was given.

subject: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996)
object: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996) described the clinical features of 17 patients from 12 Japanese families with autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism (AR-JP). There was female predominance, mean age at onset was 27.8 years, and progression was slow. The parkinsonian triad of tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia was mild, whereas gait freezing, hyperreflexia, foot dystonia, and retropulsion were relatively prominent.

subject: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996)
object: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996) found that all 17 patients with AR-JP had amelioration of parkinsonian symptoms after sleep, which they considered a characteristic finding.

subject: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996)
object: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996) reported that response to levodopa in AR-JP patients was satisfactory, but levodopa-induced choreic limb dyskinesia and the wearing-off phenomenon occurred frequently.

subject: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996)
object: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996) strongly suspected autosomal recessive inheritance of juvenile parkinsonism in their 12 Japanese families because the parents were consanguineous in all but 1 family and all patients were in a single generation.

subject: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996)
object: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996) concluded that AR-JP is a distinct clinical entity within juvenile parkinsonism. They based this on the similar clinical findings among their patients and the differences from other types of parkinsonism.

subject: Matsumine et al. (1997)
object: Matsumine et al. (1997) found a family with autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism (AR-JP) in which the disease segregated perfectly with a diallelic polymorphism of the Mn-superoxide dismutase gene (SOD2). Extending linkage analysis to 13 families with AR-JP, they mapped the AR-JP gene to chromosome 6q25.2-27, including the SOD2 locus, with maximum cumulative pairwise lod scores of 7.26 at D6S305 (theta = 0.03) and 7.71 at D6S253 (theta = 0.02). Obligate recombination events and multipoint linkage analysis placed the gene in a 17-cM interval between D6S437 and D6S264.

subject: Matsumine et al. (1997)
object: Matsumine et al. (1997) described autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism as a levodopa-responsive parkinsonism whose pathologic finding is a highly selective degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the zona compacta of the substantia nigra.

subject: Kitada et al. (1998)
object: Kitada et al. (1998) noted that AR-JP had been mapped to 6q25.2-q27 and was strongly linked to markers D6S305 and D6S253, and that D6S305 was deleted in 1 Japanese AR-JP patient. They used positional cloning within this microdeletion to isolate the causative gene.

subject: Kitada et al. (1998)
object: Kitada et al. (1998) isolated a 2,960-bp cDNA with a 1,395-bp open reading frame. It encoded a 465-amino acid protein with moderate similarity to ubiquitin at the N terminus and a RING-finger motif at the C terminus. They named the protein 'Parkin'. A 4.5-kb transcript was expressed in many human tissues and was abundant in brain, including the substantia nigra.

subject: Kitada et al. (1998)
object: Kitada et al. (1998) found that the parkin gene spans more than 500 kb and contains 12 exons.

subject: Kitada et al. (1998)
object: Kitada et al. (1998) found a deletion of exons 3 through 7 of the parkin gene in a Japanese AR-JP patient who carried a microdeletion at D6S305.

subject: Kitada et al. (1998)
object: Kitada et al. (1998) found a deletion affecting only exon 4 of the parkin gene in 4 AR-JP patients from 3 unrelated families. In brain tissue from 1 group of exon-4-deleted patients, the 4.5-kb parkin transcript was shorter. The authors concluded that mutations in parkin appear to be responsible for AR-JP.

subject: PRKN deletion affecting exon 4

subject: Matsumine et al. (1998)
object: Matsumine et al. (1998) described early-onset parkinsonism with diurnal fluctuation (EPDF) as a dopa-responsive parkinsonism with early onset in which parkinsonian symptoms improved after sleep. In a pathologic study of one EPDF case, they found selective neuronal degeneration in the zona compacta of the substantia nigra without Lewy body formation.

subject: Matsumine et al. (1998)
object: Matsumine et al. (1998) studied 53 members of 17 EPDF families (151 meioses). Multipoint linkage analysis gave a peak lod score of 14.2 at 1.0 cM telomeric to D6S305 and placed the disease locus in a 17-cM interval between D6S437 and D6S253, the same position mapped for autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism (ARJP). The highest two-point lod score was 10.13 at theta = 0 for D6S305, and haplotype analysis agreed with the multipoint result.

subject: Matsumine et al. (1998)
object: Matsumine et al. (1998) found that 8 of the 17 EPDF families were nonconsanguineous, that the families shared no common haplotypes, and that the families came from widely separated geographic origins. They suggested that EPDF has multiple founder mutations.

subject: Matsumine et al. (1998)
object: Matsumine et al. (1998) concluded that EPDF and ARJP are allelic disorders and should be included in the spectrum of a single clinicogenetic entity, chromosome 6q-linked parkinsonism. They described this disease as having a benign clinical course and relatively selective degeneration of nigral dopaminergic neurons without Lewy body formation.

subject: Saito et al. (1998)
object: Saito et al. (1998) narrowed the AR-JP locus on chromosome 6q25.2-27 by linkage analysis with densely spaced markers. The highest cumulative pairwise lod score was 9.13 at D6S1579 (theta = 0.05), and the highest cumulative multipoint lod score was 12.4 at a locus 3 cM telomeric to D6S1599. Obligate recombination events reduced the candidate region to 13 cM between D6S1579 and D6S264.

subject: Saito et al. (1998)
object: Saito et al. (1998) found strong linkage disequilibrium between the AR-JP locus and 2 markers: D6S1579 (chi-square 84.22, P < 0.0001; lambda = 0.40) and D6S1599 (chi-square 63.37, P < 0.0001; lambda = 0.30). They suggested that the AR-JP gene most likely lies near the 4-cM region containing these 2 markers.

subject: Saito et al. (1998)
object: Saito et al. (1998) described autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism as a hereditary neurodegenerative disorder with parkinsonism that responds to levodopa. Mean age at onset was 23.2 years.

subject: Tassin et al. (1998)
object: Tassin et al. (1998) tested 1 Algerian and 10 European multiplex families with early-onset Parkinson disease for linkage to the AR-JP locus on chromosome 6q25.2-q27 using marker D6S305. Homogeneity analysis gave a conditional probability in favor of linkage of greater than 0.9 in 8 families. These 8 families were analyzed further with 8 microsatellite markers spanning the 17-cM region. Haplotype reconstruction and the smallest region of homozygosity in 2 consanguineous families reduced the candidate interval to 11.3 cM.

subject: Tassin et al. (1998)
object: In the Algerian family, Tassin et al. (1998) found a deletion of 2 microsatellite markers, D6S411 and D6S1550, which colocalize on the genetic map and segregated with the disease. The title describes this as a small homozygous deletion. The authors noted that if this deletion is taken into account, the candidate region would be reduced to less than 1 cM.

subject: Tassin et al. (1998)
object: Tassin et al. (1998) confirmed linkage of AR-JP to the PARK2 locus in European families and in an Algerian family. They concluded that PARK2 appears to be an important locus for AR-JP in European patients. Linkage was favored in 8 of the 11 families tested.

subject: Tassin et al. (1998)
object: Tassin et al. (1998) found that the clinical spectrum of chromosome 6-linked AR early-onset parkinsonism in their families was broader than previously reported. Age at onset was up to 58 years, and some patients had painful dystonia.

subject: Jones et al. (1998)
object: Jones et al. (1998) found linkage of autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism to 6q25.2-q27 in 15 families from four distinct ethnic backgrounds. A full genomic screen excluded other candidate regions. Using a detailed genetic map of the linked region, they found that recombination events restricted the JP locus to a 6.9-cM region.

subject: Jones et al. (1998)
object: Jones et al. (1998) mapped the manganese superoxide dismutase gene (SOD2), a candidate gene, within the linked region, and recombination events excluded SOD2 as the JP gene.

subject: Jones et al. (1998)
object: Jones et al. (1998) observed apparent homozygosity for null alleles at marker D6S955 in one family, which suggested a deletion and finer localization of the JP locus.

subject: Mori et al. (1998)
object: Mori et al. (1998) reported pathologic and biochemical studies in a patient with 6q-linked autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism (AR-JP). Neuronal loss and gliosis were confined to the substantia nigra and the locus ceruleus, and no Lewy bodies were found. Neurofibrillary tangles and argyrophilic astrocytes were seen in the cerebral cortex and brainstem nuclei, which the authors said had not been reported before in AR-JP.

subject: Mori et al. (1998)
object: Mori et al. (1998) suggested that the finding of neurofibrillary tangles and argyrophilic astrocytes in their patient pointed to pathologic heterogeneity in 6q-linked AR-JP.

subject: Klein et al. (2000)
object: Klein et al. (2000) described a large pedigree from South Tyrol, northern Italy, with adult-onset, clinically typical tremor-dominant parkinsonism that appeared to be autosomal dominant. The 4 affected male sibs could not be clinically distinguished from most patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease. None had the hallmarks reported with earlier parkin mutations: diurnal fluctuations, benefit from sleep, foot dystonia, hyperreflexia, or early susceptibility to levodopa-induced dyskinesias.

subject: Klein et al. (2000)
object: In this South Tyrolean family, Klein et al. (2000) used haplotype analysis to exclude linkage to the chromosome 2p, 4p and 4q regions that contain genes for autosomal dominant parkinsonism. The analysis instead implicated the parkin locus on chromosome 6q.

subject: Klein et al. (2000)
object: Klein et al. (2000) found compound heterozygous deletions in the parkin gene, one large and one truncating, in the 4 affected male sibs. Two affected women in the family carried only the truncating deletion, in the heterozygous state with an apparently normal second allele.

subject: Klein et al. (2000)
object: Klein et al. (2000) concluded that parkin mutations cause a wider range of phenotypes than previously reported. They suggested that the gene may be important in the etiology of the more common late-onset typical Parkinson disease.

subject: Hayashi et al. (2000)
object: Hayashi et al. (2000) reported a 70-year-old man with autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism (AR-JP). At age 32 years he developed a dystonic gait. Hand tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and impaired postural reflexes followed. Levodopa improved these symptoms.

subject: Hayashi et al. (2000)
object: At autopsy, Hayashi et al. (2000) found loss of pigmented neurons with gliosis in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNPC) and the locus ceruleus. In the SNPC the loss was most pronounced in the medial and ventrolateral regions. The remaining SNPC neurons had low melanin content, which was less marked in the locus ceruleus. Immunostaining for alpha-synuclein confirmed there were no Lewy bodies. The authors also found neuronal loss and fibrillary gliosis in the substantia nigra pars reticulata, which they noted had not been reported before in AR-JP.

subject: Hayashi et al. (2000)
object: Hayashi et al. (2000) found a homozygous deletion of exon 4 of the parkin gene in the autopsied patient with AR-JP and in his siblings.

subject: PRKN homozygous exon 4 deletion
object: PRKN

subject: van de Warrenburg et al. (2001)
object: van de Warrenburg et al. (2001) described a Dutch family with autosomal recessive early-onset parkinsonism. Although parkinsonism was the main clinical syndrome, the proband also had mild gait ataxia.

subject: van de Warrenburg et al. (2001)
object: On neuropathologic examination of the proband, van de Warrenburg et al. (2001) found selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, along with neuronal loss in parts of the spinocerebellar system. There were no Lewy bodies or neurofibrillary tangles, but tau pathology was present.

subject: van de Warrenburg et al. (2001)
object: In the Dutch family with autosomal recessive early-onset parkinsonism, van de Warrenburg et al. (2001) found compound heterozygous mutations in the parkin gene: a heterozygous missense mutation together with a heterozygous exon deletion.

subject: Portman et al. (2001)
object: Portman et al. (2001) used PET to measure nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and cerebral energy metabolism in 2 brothers with early-onset parkinsonism caused by mutation in the parkin gene. Cerebral energy metabolism did not differ from that in sporadic PD, but the nigrostriatal dopaminergic pattern was clearly different. The authors concluded that parkinsonism in these 2 patients was pathophysiologically different from PD.

subject: Shimura et al. (2001)
object: Shimura et al. (2001) identified a protein complex in normal human brain made up of parkin as the E3 ubiquitin ligase, UbcH7 as its associated E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme, and a new 22-kD glycosylated form of alpha-synuclein (alphaSp22) as its substrate. In an in vitro ubiquitination assay, normal parkin converted alphaSp22 into polyubiquitinated, high molecular weight species.

subject: Shimura et al. (2001)
object: Shimura et al. (2001) found that, unlike normal parkin, mutant parkin associated with autosomal recessive PD did not bind alphaSp22 and did not ubiquitinate it. In parkin-deficient PD brains, alphaSp22 accumulated in a non-ubiquitinated form. The authors concluded that loss of parkin function causes pathological accumulation of alphaSp22, and suggested that this reaction underlies the accumulation of ubiquitinated alpha-synuclein in conventional PD.

subject: Hedrich et al. (2001)
object: Hedrich et al. (2001) screened the parkin gene in 21 patients with early-onset parkinsonism. Conventional screening by SSCP and sequence analysis found 3 mutations: a single base pair substitution in exon 3 and small deletions in exon 9.

object: Hedrich et al. (2001) used quantitative duplex real-time PCR to find parkin gene dosage changes in 7 of 21 patients with early-onset parkinsonism. These included heterozygous and compound heterozygous deletions of exons 2, 3, 5, and 7, a homozygous exon 7 deletion, and 2 heterozygous duplications of exon 4. Two patients carried more than 2 parkin mutations.

subject: Hedrich et al. (2001)
object: Hedrich et al. (2001) concluded that mutation analysis of the parkin gene should include gene dosage studies. They developed a real-time kinetic quantitative duplex PCR method, using fluorescence resonance energy transfer on the LightCycler, to screen all 12 parkin exons for deletions and duplications.

subject: Lücking et al. (2001)
object: Lücking et al. (2001) reported an Italian family in which parkinsonism caused by parkin gene mutations showed pseudo-dominant inheritance. The affected father was homozygous for a parkin mutation, the unaffected mother was a heterozygous carrier, and their affected son was a compound heterozygote. The authors concluded that pseudo-dominant inheritance of parkin mutations has to be considered in early-onset parkinsonism.

subject: Lücking et al. (2001)
object: In the Italian family reported by Lücking et al. (2001), the father developed parkinsonism at age 57 years and his son at age 31 years.

subject: Lücking et al. (2001)
object: In an Italian family, Lücking et al. (2001) found that the affected father was homozygous for a triplication of parkin exon 2, a mutation the authors described as so far unique. His affected son was compound heterozygous for this triplication and for a deletion of exons 3 and 4. The authors recommended sensitive screening methods such as semiquantitative multiplex PCR.

subject: Lücking et al. (2001)
object: Lücking et al. (2001) found that the unaffected mother in an Italian family was heterozygous for a deletion of parkin exons 3 and 4. Her affected son was compound heterozygous for this deletion and for the paternal exon 2 triplication.

subject: Farrer et al. (2001)
object: Farrer et al. (2001) sequenced the parkin gene in 38 patients with early-onset Parkinson disease (onset before age 41 years) and followed up 2 probands with mutations. Haplotype analysis of the 2 families showed a shared chromosome 6 carrying a novel 40-bp deletion in exon 3, which cosegregated with disease.

subject: Farrer et al. (2001)
object: Farrer et al. (2001) found that the proband of the smaller kindred carried an R275W substitution in exon 7 of the parkin gene along with the 40-bp exon 3 deletion. RNA analysis showed that the 2 mutations were on different transcripts, consistent with compound heterozygosity.

subject: Farrer et al. (2001)
object: Farrer et al. (2001) found Lewy body pathology typical of idiopathic Parkinson disease at autopsy in the compound heterozygous proband from the smaller kindred. Classically, parkin-related disease had been associated with loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and locus ceruleus without Lewy bodies.

subject: Farrer et al. (2001)
object: Farrer et al. (2001) suggested that compound heterozygous parkin mutations and loss of parkin protein may lead to early-onset parkinsonism with Lewy body pathology. They also suggested that a hemizygous (single heterozygous) mutation may increase susceptibility to typical Parkinson disease.

subject: Hoenicka et al. (2002)
object: Hoenicka et al. (2002) studied 19 Spanish kindreds with familial Parkinson disease: 13 with recessive inheritance, 4 with dominant inheritance and 2 with uncertain inheritance. Using SSCP, direct sequencing and restriction digestion of PCR-amplified genomic DNA, they found 5 different parkin (Park2) mutations in 5 of the 13 recessive families. These were deletions of exons 3 and 5, 225delA, and the novel mutations V56E and C212Y. The authors concluded that Park2 mutations account for 38% of families with recessive parkinsonism in Spain.

subject: Hoenicka et al. (2002)
object: Hoenicka et al. (2002) found that heterozygous carriers of a single Park2 mutation were either asymptomatic or developed symptoms in late adulthood or after brief exposure to haloperidol. Two simple heterozygous carriers were symptomatic. The authors suggested that heterozygous mutations could be a risk factor for parkinsonism.

subject: Hoenicka et al. (2002)
object: Hoenicka et al. (2002) found no previously described alpha-synuclein (Park1) or UCHL1 (Park5) mutations in any of the 19 Spanish families with familial Parkinson disease.

subject: Foroud et al. (2003)
object: Foroud et al. (2003) screened the parkin gene by quantitative PCR and exon sequencing in families with at least 2 sibs with PD. The families screened had either early-onset PD (onset at or before age 50 years) or a positive lod score with a marker in parkin intron 7. They identified 25 different parkin mutations in 103 individuals from 47 families. Forty-one individuals had mutations in both parkin alleles, and 62 had a single mutation in only 1 allele.

subject: Foroud et al. (2003)
object: Of the 103 individuals with parkin mutations reported by Foroud et al. (2003), 35 (34%) had onset of PD at age 60 years or older. Thirty of these 35 (86%) had a detectable mutation on only 1 parkin allele. The authors concluded that parkin mutations occur in familial PD with older onset, and that heterozygosity for a parkin mutation leads to later-onset PD. Few significant clinical differences were seen among individuals with 2, 1, or no mutated parkin copies.

subject: Oliveira et al. (2003)
object: Oliveira et al. (2003) noted that they had previously detected linkage of idiopathic Parkinson disease to the chromosome 6 region containing the Parkin gene (D6S305, lod score 5.47) in families with at least one subject with age at onset younger than 40 years.

subject: Oliveira et al. (2003)
object: Oliveira et al. (2003) screened the Parkin gene in 174 multiplex families from a genomic screen and in 133 additional Parkinson disease families. They found mutations in 18% of early-onset families and 2% of late-onset families (5% of all families screened). Age at onset in patients with Parkin mutations ranged from 12 to 71 years. Excluding exon 7 mutations, the mean age at onset was 31.5 years.

subject: Oliveira et al. (2003)
object: Oliveira et al. (2003) found that mutations in Parkin exon 7, the first RING finger (cys253 to trp, arg256 to cys, arg275 to trp, and asp280 to asn), occurred mainly in heterozygous Parkinson disease patients with a much later age at onset (mean 49.2 years). These mutations were not found in controls in this study or in several previous reports (920 chromosomes). The authors suggested that heterozygous Parkin mutations, especially those in exon 7, act as susceptibility alleles for late-onset Parkinson disease.

subject: Lohmann et al. (2003)
object: Lohmann et al. (2003) compared the phenotype of 146 patients with early-onset parkinsonism carrying parkin mutations with that of 250 patients without parkin mutations. Although no single sign distinguished the groups, patients with mutations had significantly earlier and more symmetrical onset, dystonia more often at onset, hyperreflexia, slower disease progression, and a tendency toward a greater response to levodopa despite lower doses.

subject: Lohmann et al. (2003)
object: Lohmann et al. (2003) found by forward stepwise multiple logistic regression that dystonia at onset and brisk reflexes were no longer significantly different between parkin carriers and noncarriers but correlated with age at onset rather than with parkin mutation status. Among parkin mutation carriers, age at onset varied, as did rate of progression: the younger the age at onset, the slower the evolution.

subject: Lohmann et al. (2003)
object: Lohmann et al. (2003) found that carriers of at least one parkin missense mutation had a higher UPDRS motor score than those carrying two truncating mutations, and that missense mutations in functional domains of parkin resulted in earlier onset.

subject: Lohmann et al. (2003)
object: Lohmann et al. (2003) found that patients with a single heterozygous parkin mutation had significantly later and more asymmetrical onset and more frequent levodopa-induced fluctuations and dystonia than patients with two mutations.

subject: Poorkaj et al. (2004)
object: Poorkaj et al. (2004) screened all 12 exons of the parkin gene by sequencing and dosage analysis in 39 movement disorder clinic patients with PD onset at or before 40 years of age and found mutations in 7 patients: 2 were compound heterozygous and 5 were heterozygous. Mutations included deletions of exons 2, 3, and 8, duplications of exons 2-4 and 9, and a P437L substitution; 78% of mutations were deletions/multiplications. None of the point mutations found in patients were detected in 96 controls.

subject: Poorkaj et al. (2004)
object: Poorkaj et al. (2004) found that phenotypes of parkin mutation carriers were consistent with idiopathic PD, so that parkin cases could present as typical idiopathic PD distinguishable only by molecular testing.

subject: Poorkaj et al. (2004)
object: Poorkaj et al. (2004) found that in the clinic setting 10% of PD patients had early-onset disease and 18% of these had parkin mutations, but if parkin is recessive only 5% of early-onset cases, those with compound mutations, could be attributed to this locus. The mutation frequency was 0.12 (95% CI 0.04-0.19), and 70% of parkin cases were heterozygous; the authors stated that it was unclear whether heterozygous mutations are pathogenic.

subject: Poorkaj et al. (2004)
object: Poorkaj et al. (2004) concluded that parkin-based diagnosis and counseling require a better understanding of the mode of inheritance, penetrance, and carrier frequencies.

subject: Sasaki et al. (2004)
object: Sasaki et al. (2004) reported autopsy findings in a patient with autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism. Brain lesions were limited to dopaminergic neuron systems such as the substantia nigra and locus ceruleus. Melanin-containing neurons in the pars compacta of the substantia nigra were moderately to severely depleted, with gliosis. Neurons in the locus ceruleus were mildly decreased, and melanin pigment was seen outside neurons.

subject: Sasaki et al. (2004)
object: Sasaki et al. (2004) found no Lewy bodies in the neuropil of the substantia nigra pars compacta or the locus ceruleus. Basophilic inclusion bodies were seen only occasionally, in the neuropil of the pedunculopontine nucleus. These inclusions were doughnut-shaped or round and stained positive for alpha-synuclein and ubiquitin. The authors concluded that different parkin gene abnormalities may lead to differences in the degree and distribution of neuronal degeneration, including whether Lewy bodies are present. They also suggested that parkin-induced parkinsonism may be related to idiopathic Parkinson disease.

subject: Sasaki et al. (2004)
object: Sasaki et al. (2004) reported that their autopsied patient with autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism carried a homozygous deletion of exon 3 in the parkin gene.

subject: Khan et al. (2005)
object: Khan et al. (2005) used 18F-dopa PET to study 13 unrelated asymptomatic heterozygous carriers of a single parkin mutation. Compared with control subjects, the carriers had significantly reduced 18F-dopa uptake in the caudate, putamen, and ventral and dorsal midbrain. Four of the carriers had subtle extrapyramidal signs.

subject: Khan et al. (2005)
object: Khan et al. (2005) concluded that being heterozygous for a parkin mutation is a risk factor for nigrostriatal dysfunction. They suggested that in some carriers it may contribute to late-onset Parkinson disease, even though parkin disease is usually autosomal recessive.

subject: Ohsawa et al. (2005)
object: Ohsawa et al. (2005) performed nerve conduction studies in 9 PARK2 patients and 8 patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease and found a significant reduction of sural sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) amplitude in 8 of the PARK2 patients, most of whom were asymptomatic. The authors suggested that sensory axonal neuropathy may be a common clinical feature of PARK2.

subject: Ohsawa et al. (2005)
object: Ohsawa et al. (2005) suggested that a reduced amplitude of the sural SNAP could be a diagnostic indicator of PARK2.

subject: Pramstaller et al. (2005)
object: Pramstaller et al. (2005) reported a 7-generation pedigree of 196 individuals, 25 of whom had levodopa-responsive parkinsonism. Parkin mutations were found in 77 subjects. Of the 25 patients, 5 carried compound heterozygous mutations and met UK PD Society Brain Bank criteria for definite Parkinson disease. Eight carried only a heterozygous Parkin mutation, 7 had no Parkin mutation, and the status of 5 deceased patients was unknown.

subject: Pramstaller et al. (2005)
object: In this pedigree, Pramstaller et al. (2005) found that age at onset differed significantly between patients with compound heterozygous Parkin mutations and both heterozygous carriers and patients without detectable Parkin mutations. The authors suggested the pedigree offered a chance to study heterozygous Parkin mutations as a risk factor for PD.

subject: Pramstaller et al. (2005)
object: Pramstaller et al. (2005) identified compound heterozygous Parkin mutations, a deletion of exon 7 and del1072T, in a 73-year-old patient from the large pedigree. Both mutations deleted the In-Between-RING (IBR) domain.

subject: Pramstaller et al. (2005)
object: In a 73-year-old compound heterozygous Parkin mutation carrier, Pramstaller et al. (2005) found at autopsy PD-type cell loss, reactive gliosis, and alpha-synuclein-positive Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra and locus ceruleus. Surviving neurons reacted with antibodies to the Parkin N terminus but not to the IBR domain.

subject: Chien et al. (2006)
object: Chien et al. (2006) described a genetic isolate from north-eastern Brazil in which genealogical studies connected 255 individuals, 15 of whom had Parkinson disease. DNA was obtained from 10 early-onset PD patients, 1 case with likely neuroleptic-induced parkinsonism, and 15 unaffected relatives. The average age at onset of PD symptoms was 30.8 years (range, 12 to 46 years).

subject: Chien et al. (2006)
object: Chien et al. (2006) noted that geographic isolation and multiple consanguineous marriages in the Brazilian kindred initially suggested autosomal recessive inheritance, and haplotype analysis revealed homozygosity in the PD patients for markers across the PARK2 locus.

subject: Chien et al. (2006)
object: In 10 patients with early-onset PD from a Brazilian genetic isolate, Chien et al. (2006) identified a novel homozygous splice-site mutation in the parkin gene (IVS1+1G-T) that completely cosegregated with the phenotype. cDNA analysis showed total loss of parkin transcript in homozygous carriers, indicating a loss-of-function mutation.

subject: PRKN IVS1 + 1G/T
object: PRKN

subject: Chien et al. (2006)
object: Chien et al. (2006) found that the case with neuroleptic-induced parkinsonism and 13 of 15 healthy relatives were heterozygous carriers of the IVS1+1G-T parkin mutation. The absence of PD in heterozygotes indicated a genuinely recessive mutation, suggesting that parkin haploinsufficiency is not a relevant risk factor for early- or late-onset PD, although the authors suggested it could facilitate neuroleptic-induced parkinsonism.

subject: Kay et al. (2007)
object: Kay et al. (2007) sequenced the parkin gene in 302 patients with Parkinson disease and 301 control subjects, with replication in 1,260 additional patients and 1,657 control subjects. They detected 34 variants, 21 of them novel; 12 were polymorphisms and 22 were rare variants. Patients and controls did not differ in the frequency, type, or functional location of the variants.

subject: Kay et al. (2007)
object: Kay et al. (2007) found the P437L parkin variant, a common mutation thought to be pathogenic, in unaffected control subjects.

subject: Kay et al. (2007)
object: Kay et al. (2007) concluded that parkin point mutations are not exclusive to Parkinson disease and that a single point mutation in a patient, in the absence of a second mutation, should not be taken as a cause of disease unless corroborated by family data and functional studies. Their study did not support heterozygous parkin sequence variants as risk factors for PD; whether heterozygous dosage anomalies are associated with PD remained to be determined.

subject: Wang et al. (2008)
object: Wang et al. (2008) screened the Parkin gene for point mutations and exon deletions and duplications in 247 probands with Parkinson disease (onset at or before age 50 years) and 104 control probands enrolled in the Genetic Epidemiology of Parkinson's Disease (GEPD) study. They found Parkin mutations in 25 probands with PD (10.1%). Eighteen of these 25 (72.0%) were heterozygotes, and 1 Parkin homozygote was reported in 2 sibs with PD.

subject: Wang et al. (2008)
object: Wang et al. (2008) used the kin-cohort method to estimate the cumulative incidence of PD to age 65 years in first-degree relatives who carried Parkin mutations (age-specific penetrance). The estimate was 7.0% (95% CI, 0.4-71.9%), compared with 1.7% in noncarrier relatives of cases (P = 0.59) and 1.1% in relatives of controls. They concluded that the risk in noncarrier relatives of early-onset cases was not significantly greater than the general population risk among controls, and that age-specific penetrance among Parkin carriers, particularly heterozygotes, deserved further study.

subject: Mortiboys et al. (2008)
object: Mortiboys et al. (2008) studied skin fibroblasts from 5 patients with early-onset parkinsonism and homozygous or compound heterozygous parkin mutations, identified by direct sequencing and MLPA gene dosage analysis. Genotypes included 255delA with exon 5 deletion; homozygous 202_203delAG (exon 2); 202_203delAG with exon 2 deletion; 202_203delAG with exon 4 deletion; and c.101-102delAG (p.Gln34ArgfsX38) with c.1289G>A (p.Gly430Asp).

subject: Mortiboys et al. (2008)
object: Mortiboys et al. (2008) found that fibroblasts from 5 parkin-mutant patients had mitochondrial membrane potential reduced by about 30% in glucose medium and 70% in galactose medium, complex I activity reduced by about 42%, with normal complex III and IV activity, reduced complex I-linked (but not complex II-linked) ATP production, and a 58% reduction in cellular ATP levels. Cell viability and growth were unaffected.

subject: Mortiboys et al. (2008)
object: Mortiboys et al. (2008) observed increased mitochondrial branching in parkin-mutant fibroblasts, which correlated with lower complex I-linked ATP production and lower complex I activity, suggesting that the functional and morphological effects of parkin deficiency on mitochondria are related. FRAP assays showed reduced functional connectivity of the mitochondrial matrix, worsened by rotenone, and rotenone shortened mitochondria in parkin-mutant but not control cells.

subject: Mortiboys et al. (2008)
object: Mortiboys et al. (2008) showed that siRNA knockdown of parkin by 80% in control fibroblasts reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and cellular ATP and increased mitochondrial branching by 70%, indicating that parkin deficiency is sufficient to explain the patient cell defects. In contrast, 50% knockdown, mimicking haploinsufficiency, had no effect, which the authors considered consistent with true recessive inheritance and not supportive of heterozygosity as a PD risk factor.

subject: Mortiboys et al. (2008)
object: Mortiboys et al. (2008) found that treatment of parkin-mutant fibroblasts with the glutathione precursor OTCA (10 microM) restored mitochondrial membrane potential to 95% of control levels and completely restored cellular ATP, apparently via a compensatory increase in complex II activity rather than correction of the complex I defect; glutathione methyl ester gave only partial rescue (60%). They suggested patient fibroblasts could serve as a screening system for disease-modifying compounds.

subject: Marder et al. (2010)
object: Marder et al. (2010) screened the parkin gene for point mutations and exon copy number variation in 956 patients with early-onset Parkinson disease (age at onset younger than 51 years) recruited at 13 movement disorders centers in the CORE-PD study. Sixty-four patients (6.7%) had parkin mutations: 3.9% were heterozygous, 0.6% homozygous, and 2.2% compound heterozygous. Copy number variation was present in 52.3% of mutation carriers (31.6% of heterozygotes, 83.3% of homozygotes, and 81.0% of compound heterozygotes). No consanguinity was reported.

subject: Marder et al. (2010)
object: Marder et al. (2010) found that the prevalence of parkin mutations fell as age at onset rose: 57% (8/14) with onset before age 20, 30% (13/43) at ages 20 to 29, 9% (23/254) at ages 30 to 39, and 3% (20/644) at ages 40 to 50. Every carrier group had a younger mean age at onset than noncarriers (heterozygotes 37.2 years, homozygotes 28.5, compound heterozygotes 28.9, noncarriers 42.0). Compound heterozygotes and homozygotes each had a significantly younger age at onset than heterozygotes. Onset before age 40 was associated with carrying any parkin mutation (OR 5.0), and compared with heterozygotes, younger onset was associated with carrying 2 mutations (OR 6.6).

subject: Marder et al. (2010)
object: Marder et al. (2010) found that patients with a parkin mutation in the heterozygous state had a younger age at onset than noncarriers after adjustment for ethnicity and family history. The authors concluded that this supports parkin heterozygosity being a susceptibility factor for PD. A family history of PD in a first-degree relative was associated with carrying any parkin mutation (OR 2.8): 11.8% of patients with a family history carried mutations, compared with 5.7% of those without one.

subject: Marder et al. (2010)
object: In the early-onset PD cohort studied by Marder et al. (2010), dystonia as a presenting sign did not differ between parkin mutation carriers (0%) and noncarriers (1.7%). Response to levodopa was also similar: 93.4% of carriers and 90.5% of noncarriers reported a response to antiparkinson medication.

subject: Marder et al. (2010)
object: Marder et al. (2010) found that Hispanic ethnicity was associated with carrying a parkin mutation (15.6% of Hispanic patients vs 5.7% of white non-Hispanic patients; OR 2.7). None of the 12 Black non-Hispanic patients carried a mutation. Of the 12 Hispanic carriers, 7 were Puerto Rican. Six Hispanic patients (5 Puerto Rican and 1 Mexican) carried a deletion of exons 3-4, and both exon 3-4 homozygotes were of Puerto Rican descent. The second most common mutation in Hispanics was 255delA, found in 3 Puerto Ricans together with the exon 3-4 deletion and in 1 Mexican heterozygote; it was not detected in 139 Caribbean Hispanic controls.

(2010) identified recurrent combinations including 255delA plus an exon 3-4 deletion (3 Hispanic patients) and Arg275Trp with a variety of second alleles. Arg275Trp was also the most frequent heterozygous mutation, found in 8 patients. Other mutations found included Arg42Pro, Gly430Asp, and an exon 3 40-bp deletion.

subject: Alcalay et al. (2010)
object: Alcalay et al. (2010) screened 953 patients with early-onset Parkinson disease (age at onset 50 years or younger) from 13 movement disorders centers of the CORE-PD study, recruited regardless of family history, for mutations in SNCA, PRKN, PINK1, DJ1, LRRK2, and GBA. In the Results, 33 patients were PRKN heterozygotes and 27 were PRKN homozygotes or compound heterozygotes. The abstract gives 64 (6.7%) PRKN carriers. Hispanic patients were more likely than non-Hispanic patients to carry PRKN mutations (15.6% vs 5.9%, P = 0.003).

subject: Alcalay et al. (2010)
object: Alcalay et al. (2010) found that age at onset was significantly younger in PRKN mutation carriers than in carriers of all other mutations (P < 0.001). Mean age at onset was 29 years in carriers of 2 PRKN mutations and 37 years in PRKN heterozygotes, compared with 42 years in noncarriers. Patients with 2 PRKN mutations made up 35% of cases with onset at age 20 or younger, 17% with onset at 21 to 30 years, and 0.5% with onset at 41 to 50 years.

subject: Alcalay et al. (2010)
object: Alcalay et al. (2010) found that PRKN carriers were more likely than LRRK2 carriers to report a family history of PD, even though PRKN-related disease is considered recessive. The authors suggested that the high frequency of PRKN heterozygotes may support the idea that even a single PRKN mutation is a risk factor for early-onset PD.

subject: Alcalay et al. (2010)
object: Alcalay et al. (2010) described 3 patients with early-onset PD who were heterozygous for a PRKN mutation and also carried a GBA mutation: an exon 2 deletion plus GBA L444P, R275W plus GBA L444P, and D53E plus GBA N370S. A fourth patient, of Jewish ancestry, carried a heterozygous PRKN exon 5-6 deletion together with LRRK2 G2019S. None of these patients reported Parkinson disease in a first-degree relative.

subject: Kay et al. (2010)
object: Kay et al. (2010) screened 2,091 patients with Parkinson disease (mean onset age 58.3 years) and 1,686 controls for PARK2 deletions, multiplications, and copy number variations (CNVs), using semiquantitative PCR and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification, with validation by real-time quantitative PCR. The subjects had already been tested for point mutations. Thirteen patients had 2 CNV mutations, 5 had 1 CNV plus 1 point mutation, and 18 had 1 CNV mutation. The mutations found in patients spanned exons 2-9.

subject: Kay et al. (2010)
object: Kay et al. (2010) found heterozygous PARK2 CNV mutations in 0.95% of 1,686 controls and 0.86% of 2,091 patients with Parkinson disease. All of the CNV mutations in the 16 carrier controls were in exons 1-4, which spare the exons encoding functionally critical protein domains.

subject: Kay et al. (2010)
object: In white subjects, Kay et al. (2010) found that carrying 1 PARK2 CNV did not increase the risk of Parkinson disease (odds ratio 1.05, p = 0.89) and was not associated with earlier onset (64.7 years in heterozygotes vs 58.5 years in noncarriers). They concluded that there was no compelling evidence that heterozygous PARK2 mutations, alone or combined with known risk factors (SNCA, MAPT, APOE, smoking, coffee intake), are associated with PD.

subject: Alcalay et al. (2011)
object: Alcalay et al. (2011) gave the University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT) to 44 probands from the CORE-PD study whose Parkinson disease began at or before age 50 years. Of these, 9 were Parkin compound heterozygotes, 10 were heterozygotes and 25 were noncarriers. Compound heterozygotes had higher UPSIT scores (31.9) than heterozygotes (20.1) or noncarriers (19.9) (p less than 0.001), and this difference persisted after adjustment for age, gender, disease duration and smoking. The authors concluded that compound heterozygotes with PD have olfaction within the normal range.

subject: Alcalay et al. (2011)
object: Alcalay et al. (2011) found that olfaction was significantly reduced in PD patients who were heterozygous for a single Parkin mutation but not in their heterozygous relatives without PD. Among relatives without PD, UPSIT scores were similar in heterozygotes (32.5) and noncarriers (32.4), and better than in heterozygotes with PD (p = 0.001). The authors stated that further research is required to assess whether these findings reflect different neuropathology in Parkin mutation heterozygotes and compound heterozygotes.

subject: Zhu et al. (2022)
object: Zhu et al. (2022) evaluated PRKN mutations, including SNVs and copy number variants, in the UK Biobank (whole exome sequencing and genotyping array data from 200,606 participants) and found a pathogenic PRKN mutation in 1.8% of participants and 2 mutations in approximately 1 in 7,800 participants.

subject: Zhu et al. (2022)
object: Zhu et al. (2022) found that UK Biobank participants carrying 1 pathogenic PRKN variant were as likely as noncarriers to have Parkinson disease (OR 0.91, 0.58-1.38; P = 0.76) or a parent with Parkinson disease (OR 1.12; P = 0.19); similarly, in the NIH-PD + AMP-PD case-control cohort (whole genome sequencing of 4,094 participants), heterozygous carriers were not at increased risk (OR 1.29, 0.74-2.38; P = 0.43). The authors concluded that heterozygous pathogenic PRKN mutations are common but do not increase the risk of Parkinson disease.

subject: Zhu et al. (2022)
object: Zhu et al. (2022) identified 2,692 PRKN copy number variants from genotyping array data in the UK Biobank; deletions or duplications involving exon 2 accounted for roughly half of all CNVs, and 88% involved exons 2, 3, or 4. Using NIH-PD participants genotyped by whole genome sequencing, array, and MLPA, they validated genotyping arrays for CNV detection.

subject: Zhu et al. (2022)
object: In the NIH-PD cohort, Zhu et al. (2022) used functional assays of patient fibroblasts to resolve variants of unclear significance in biallelic PRKN carriers, and the results suggested that cryptic loss-of-function variants in monoallelic carriers are not a substantial confounder for association studies.
